name: Screen Studio
subcategory: screen recording, walkthroughs and product demos
tagline: Record a Mac screen and automatically apply cursor zoom, padding, and smooth framing

pricing.notes: Sold primarily as a one-time license; priceMonthly is null by design.

tiers.name: Screen Studio
tiers.limits: All recording and editing features; share links; exports up to 4K/60fps
tiers.notes: The live page now sells a subscription; previously purchased one-time licenses remain governed by their original terms.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no permanent free tier; a download/trial is offered but its numeric limits and duration are not publicly stated
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; annual rate displayed as $9/month
pricing.hiddenCosts: Current access is subscription-based rather than a new lifetime license; the public page does not state storage or fair-use caps for hosted share links.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Screen Studio, record a Mac screen and automatically apply cursor zoom, padding, and smooth framing. The hard boundary is exceptional macos capture polish, motion design, and ongoing compatibility, plus capture polish, hosting, and collaboration.
coreLoopDIY: Record a Mac screen with microphone audio, automatically apply cursor zoom, padding, and smooth framing, trim the result, and export a shareable local video.
whatYouLose: exceptional macOS capture polish, motion design, and ongoing compatibility
ongoingBurden: OS permissions, codecs, rendering performance, uploads, storage, links, and viewer analytics
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Screen Studio because the recording itself is easy; the subscription removes upload, transcoding, sharing, organization, and support work. The recurring cost buys OS permissions, codecs, rendering performance, uploads, storage, links, and viewer analytics, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Cap
priorArt.desc: Open-source screen recording and sharing product with modern desktop architecture.

alternatives.name: Recordly
alternatives.desc: Auto-zoom demos with styled frames and installers; young enough that audio still occasionally picks a fight.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Screenize
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Promising Screen Studio clone whose maintainer explicitly paused development in May 2026.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Lifetime license plan and a personal desktop recorder DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Screen Studio in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, ffmpeg, and SQLite; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: record a Mac screen with microphone audio, automatically apply cursor zoom, padding, and smooth framing, trim the result, and export a shareable local video.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Offer screen, window, or region capture plus optional microphone audio.
Show an always-visible recording timer and make stop available from the tray.
Create a non-destructive trim view with crop, zoom, cursor highlight, and text callouts.
Render locally through ffmpeg with sensible H.264 and WebM presets.
Generate a poster frame, transcript, and Markdown summary beside each video.
Provide copy-file-path and reveal-in-folder actions instead of mandatory cloud upload.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out public cloud hosting.
Deliberately leave out viewer identity and engagement analytics.
Deliberately leave out enterprise workspaces and SSO.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
